name: Yusuf Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the trombone section for a touring youth orchestra, teach four advanced brass pupils and write short horn charts, the written parts players follow, for a local theatre. My music master’s and years of auditions made me a strong player, but the contract pays less than most people think a section lead earns.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part do you enjoy, and what strains home life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a young player hears the rest of the brass breathe with them. The tour bus returns after our children’s bedtime; my partner works shifts at a bakery and covers school pickup when the rota allows. We have a mortgage, under a month saved and few similar posts nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that faster route sheets are useful, but someone still has to count the young players onto the bus. A cheaper calendar does not pay for another rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We are paid below what this leading job usually brings, and the mortgage has no spare month behind it. Even without radical AI, a cancelled tour day and a short bakery week would put us behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the paid tour rehearsals and four pupils this season. I already use AI each day to transpose a practice line, meaning move it into a different musical key, but I play it at the trombone before sending it; if a tour date cancels, I would skip the rented rehearsal booth for that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a missed tour fee, whatever happens with AI. The next mortgage payment arrives faster than the next booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a tour date lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school hall closed for repairs last spring and our contract paid no cancellation fee. I would ask the organiser for a written half-day fee before the next tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the pupils learn from your checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They hear me catch an impossible low note before a chart goes home. A child should not have to practise a note the horn cannot play.

say: I would welcome **quicker route sheets** while defending paid rehearsals.
I would seek a **written cancellation fee** for the next tour.
think: Our **thin savings** cannot cover a missed tour day and short bakery week.
Senior **section work** still pays less than people assume.
do: Keep **paid tour rehearsals** and four pupils this season.
Skip **booth rental** if a tour date cancels; request a written half-day fee before next tour.
feel: I feel **anxious** because ordinary missed work can affect the mortgage.
S0.quote: A child should not have to practise a note the horn cannot play.
fieldNote: His **high skill** does not offset low pay, variable partner shifts and a reserve under one month.
Daily **AI transposition** is existing use, checked by playing at the trombone.

steps.text: Keep paid tour rehearsals and four brass pupils this season
Skip rented rehearsal booth in week a paid tour date cancels
Request written half-day cancellation fee before next tour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players that software can copy our horn charts and answer booking emails. I would ask the musicians’ association for paid preparation hours and permission before a theatre reuses our recorded parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The charts are nearly a third of my own pay, and I expect fewer orders. The orchestra might keep its live places, but our account cannot float a long stretch without chart fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would bring chart invoices to the association and learn the theatre’s new AI cue-timing checker with its sound engineer. In the first year I would use only a horn take I own, compare its marked beats with my score and the live cue, and stop if a note moves or the file leaves the theatre server; I would not upload pupil audio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed at a likely cut to that third of my pay. I can learn a new control quickly. Software cannot add money to our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for that new checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre must give the trial without a subscription charge. I would keep my own score and refuse the tool if a paid licence is required.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the fee for drawing a chart before the first rehearsal. The section leaders can ask together so one teacher is not singled out.

say: I would seek **paid chart preparation** and recording consent together.
I would explain that **cheap copied charts** shrink real musician fees.
think: My **horn charts** supply nearly a third of my own income.
Thin **household savings** cannot carry a long fall in orders.
do: Bring **chart invoices** to the association for paid preparation and reuse consent this month.
Learn the **cue checker** after engineer instruction, free trial on owned take; compare score/live cue and stop on errors or leakage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about likely lost chart pay and a mortgage-sized gap.
S1.quote: Software cannot add money to our account.
fieldNote: He learns a **new AI checker** beyond daily transposition, with engineer instruction and no paid subscription.
The trial uses an **owned horn take**, manual score/live comparison and a theatre-server privacy boundary.

steps.text: Ask musicians’ association for paid chart preparation and recording consent this month
Test free checker after engineer instruction on owned take; compare score/live cue, stop on errors/leakage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the youth orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make the charts and route plans cheaply. Playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later, and those years do not protect my chart invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect chart orders to disappear in 2028 and some paid planning hours to fall. The bakery rota cannot cover our mortgage and two children if a third of my pay goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would get signed tour dates and add the chart invoices to our household budget. In the first year after 2028, if chart orders stop, I would ask the lender before arrears for full written interest and fees on any temporary plan, and apply for a posted community-music director post only if it accepts my master’s and any required teaching licence I hold, written net pay after travel and childcare beats lost chart fees, and school pickup works. I would keep the tour and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about the likely loss before I can replace it. A fine audition cannot turn tomorrow’s mortgage into next month’s bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for a post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would search the few nearby jobs first. I would not move two schoolchildren on the hope that a distant vacancy becomes an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lender offers a smaller payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the extra interest and fees cost overall before accepting. A lower payment now can put a bigger bill on us later.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 playing robots.
I would seek **signed tour dates** and an actual paid director vacancy.
think: My **chart orders** likely end before hands-on robots arrive.
Variable **bakery pay** cannot cover our mortgage if a third of my fees vanish.
do: Get **signed tour dates** and count chart invoices now; keep tour and pupils until a written director offer.
Request **lender terms** before arrears if 2028 charts stop; review full written extra interest and fees before accepting.
Seek **posted director role** only if qualified, written net pay beats chart losses after travel/childcare and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely large income loss with almost no reserve.
S2.quote: A fine audition cannot turn tomorrow’s mortgage into next month’s bill.
fieldNote: His **2028 chart loss** comes before 2031 playing robots and threatens a third of his lower-paid music income.
A director move requires **posted work**, eligibility, written net replacement pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Keep tour rehearsals and four pupils until suitable written director offer is signed
Review full written lender interest/fees before accepting if 2028 charts stop; call before arrears
Seek qualifying posted director role if orders stop; written net-after-travel/childcare pay beats loss, pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to build brass teaching people will pay for. Playing robots follow around 2034, after the chart market changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The charts could still end in 2031. A separate weekend brass choir might replace some pay, but a room full of unpaid friends is not an income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would ask a separate neighbourhood hall for a Saturday room after the children’s sports pickup. I would run a six-week brass choir only if six adults prepay enough for the room and my conducting and preparation hours, and every shared mouthpiece is cleaned or players bring their own sound instruments. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only if six still prepay the room and my time, the room remains available after pickup and the instruments stay safe; I would keep paid tour work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the class covers my hours. A paid brass choir must cover my preparation before I can call it income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would clean a shared mouthpiece?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall must show me its cleaning plan before I collect a fee. If it cannot, players use their own safe instruments or I cancel the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if four adults sign up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees will not cover the room and my preparation. I would refund them and keep the four pupils who already pay me.

say: I would offer a **paid brass choir** only with real registrations.
I would refuse **unsafe shared instruments** in a teaching room.
think: My **chart income** may end by 2031 before 2034 playing robots.
Six **prepaid adults** must fund room and conducting preparation.
do: Start **brass choir** with six prepayments covering room and work, pickup fit, and cleaned mouthpieces or sound own instruments.
Repeat **paid choir** after 2031 only with six prepayments covering room and my time, available room, safe instruments and pickup.
Keep **paid tour work** if class fees fail.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the separate brass class pays for my time.
S3.quote: A paid brass choir must cover my preparation before I can call it income.
fieldNote: The **separate choir** needs six prepayments covering hall, conducting and preparation hours.
Shared mouthpieces need a **cleaning plan** or adults bring safe instruments; pickup must fit.

steps.text: Start brass choir if six prepay room/work, pickup fits, mouthpieces cleaned or instruments owned and safe
Renew choir after 2031 if six prepay room/time, room available, instruments safe and pickup fits
Keep paid orchestra tour dates while booked
Refund four prepayments rather than run choir without covered room and preparation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to learn a trade and ask for its pay in writing. Robots able to play a horn follow around 2039, not on the same date as chart software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still be leading brass at 53, but our mortgage is due this winter. The chart orders could end by 2036, and a senior title has not given us one month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save any extra cleared chart fee after food and mortgage toward one full month of household expenses. Through the decade I would keep the separate brass choir only while six people prepay room and conducting/preparation, a room and safe instruments are available after pickup; in the first year after 2036, if paid tour dates shrink, I would seek a posted music-director job only if it accepts my qualifications and written net pay after travel and childcare replaces lost tour pay. I would keep the tour and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious about our present bills even with ten years to prepare. A new title will not fix a month with no paid date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save a promised chart fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the client has to pay it first, and food and mortgage come before a transfer. If charts stop selling, I would save nothing from that source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another qualification now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read an actual posted director job first. I would apply only if my existing master’s and experience count, rather than buying an unfunded course on a guess.

say: I would teach the children to ask for **written pay**.
I would separate **2036 thinking AGI** from 2039 playing robots.
think: Our **mortgage** needs cash now, not in 2036.
My **senior title** has not built a full month of reserve.
do: Save **cleared extra chart fees** after essentials toward one month of expenses.
Keep the **separate brass choir** only with six prepayments covering room and my time, safe instruments, available room and pickup.
Seek **posted director job** post-2036 if pay falls; require qualification, written net pay covering losses, travel/childcare, pickup; keep work until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** because current bills remain tight despite the longer warning.
S4.quote: A new title will not fix a month with no paid date.
fieldNote: His **one-month reserve goal** uses only cleared extra chart income after essentials.
The later **director move** requires actual tour loss, a posted role, eligibility, viable written net pay and signed offer.

steps.text: Save cleared extra chart fees after food and mortgage toward one month of expenses
Keep brass choir if six prepay room/time, room available, safe instruments and pickup fits
Seek qualifying posted director role after tour cuts, with replacement written net-after-travel/childcare pay and pickup
Keep paid tour rehearsals and pupils until suitable written director offer is signed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because horn charts could stop before I replace a third of my income. Signed tour dates, a lender plan with full costs and a posted eligible director role with written net pay and workable pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the low note before a child practises it. A line can look perfect on a screen and still be impossible to play on a trombone.

headlineQuote: A line can look perfect on a screen and still be impossible to play on a trombone.
portrait: At **43**, Yusuf leads a youth-orchestra trombone section, teaches four pupils and writes horn charts with a music master’s and strong skill.
His **lower pay**, bakery shifts, mortgage, two children and less than one month saved make missed dates urgent.
He uses **AI daily** for transposition and learns a new cue checker with owned audio, engineer instruction and manual comparison.
He seeks **collective chart fees** and tests a paid brass choir only with six prepayments, safe instruments and covered pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase horn-chart fees worth a third of his income before new paid work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed tour dates**, a costed lender plan and a posted eligible director job with written net pay and pickup would help.
